title: Even Devadatta
hookLine: in the Lotus Sutra he too is promised Buddhahood, a Mahayana view (Lotus Sutra, Devadatta chapter)

cards: What happens to Devadatta in the end? The Pali commentaries tell it starkly. Late in life, tradition says, he set out to see the Buddha and ask forgiveness, and the earth opened and swallowed him before he arrived.
The same commentaries add a quieter line: far in the future, even he will come to awakening. And a Mahayana scripture, the Lotus Sutra, has a chapter that carries his name and goes further still.
It doesn't begin with Devadatta's crimes. It begins with a king, long ago, who wanted to learn.

teach.h: A KING WHO WANTED THE TEACHING.
teach.b: First, the king. In the chapter, the Buddha tells of a past life when he was a king who wanted the highest teaching so much that he was ready to give up his throne for it. He would serve anyone who could teach him.
Second, the seer. A seer came who knew a sutra, the Lotus, and would teach it if the king became his servant.
So the king picked fruit, drew water, gathered firewood, prepared food, even let his own body be the seer's seat, and never wearied of it. Third, the name.
That seer, the Buddha says, was Devadatta. Because of Devadatta, his good friend, he came to complete the qualities of a buddha. Fourth, the promise.

teach.h: HE TOO WILL BE A BUDDHA.
teach.b: After a vast stretch of time, the chapter says, Devadatta himself will become a buddha, named Heavenly King. This is a Mahayana view, and it's fair to say plainly whose it is.
Theravada Buddhists read the Pali Vinaya and commentaries, where Devadatta's deeds bring heavy results, though the commentaries also leave that far door open.
In some Mahayana schools, the Lotus chapter is read as saying no one stands outside the reach of awakening, not even the cousin who rolled the rock.

Some teachers also read it about enemies: the one who opposed you may turn out, in a long enough view, to be part of what formed you. Neither tradition says what Devadatta did was small. Both keep the warning.
The Lotus chapter sets a promise beside it.

how: In some Mahayana communities the Lotus Sutra is chanted and studied, and its Devadatta chapter is read as a teaching that awakening reaches everyone; in Theravada communities Devadatta's story is told from the Pali Vinaya and commentaries as a warning about envy and ambition.

o: Devadatta was innocent of the plots after all
even the Buddha's worst foe is promised awakening
the Buddha forgave Devadatta at their last meeting

games.q: the Devadatta chapter: tap the pairs.
p: served a seer to learn the teaching
Devadatta's future name as a buddha

s: the Lotus Sutra says what Devadatta did was harmless
it doesn't excuse him. it tells of a past life where he taught the Buddha, and promises him a far future.
in the chapter, the Buddha calls Devadatta his good friend
because of Devadatta, he says, he completed the qualities of a buddha.
the promise that Devadatta will be a buddha comes from the Pali Vinaya
it's a Mahayana view, from the Lotus Sutra. the Pali commentaries tell a harsher story, with a far door left open.

games.q: you're the king in the Buddha's story, and you want the highest teaching. a seer says he'll teach it, if you become his servant. what do you do?
o: refuse; a king serves no one.
serve him: fruit, water, firewood, whatever he needs.
send a servant in your place.
games.why: the king serves him without wearying, and learns. then the Buddha reveals the seer was Devadatta.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has opposed you, not the worst, someone in the middle: a rival, a critic, someone who made one season harder.
If you practice loving-kindness, use the phrases it already uses; if not, simply wish them one good thing, a good night's sleep or a kind word.
Wishing them well doesn't approve of what they did, just as the Lotus chapter doesn't excuse Devadatta.

wordCard.voice: Even Devadatta. In the Lotus Sutra, the cousin who split the sangha is named the Buddha's past teacher and promised buddhahood. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: the cousin's name, written in Devanagari.

carryVoice: Your line: even him. The warning stays, and a far door is left open. Day seven hundred seventy-eight, done.
